chicken-tenders-or-strips-breaded-from-f.title: Chicken tenders or strips, breaded, frozen

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tenders or strips are pieces of chicken breast coated in a breading made from flour, breadcrumbs and spices, then flash‑frozen. They are designed for quick cooking in an oven, microwave or deep‑fryer, delivering a juicy interior and a crispy exterior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The breading often includes a blend of wheat flour, cornflakes and aromatic herbs.
Freezing locks in nutrients and flavor without the need for preservatives.
Chicken tenders became a staple of fast‑food menus in the 1970s.
In many countries they are served with barbecue, honey‑mustard or sweet‑chili sauces.
A quick pre‑fry before freezing creates a golden crust that stays crisp without extra oil at home.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat when baked
items.content: Baking in the oven without added oil yields a lower‑fat product compared with deep‑frying.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It also provides iron, zinc and phosphorus important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Portion control and convenience
items.content: Pre‑portioned frozen packs make it easy to manage serving sizes.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The breading is often salted; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor salt intake.

items.title: Trans fats in some breadings
items.content: Certain ready‑made mixes may contain partially hydrogenated oils; look for trans‑fat‑free products.

items.title: Bacterial risk with improper storage
items.content: If the frozen product thaws and stays at room temperature, the risk of pathogen growth increases.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Preheat the oven to 200 °C, spread the tenders on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper and bake 12‑15 minutes until golden and crisp. They can also be microwaved (2‑3 minutes) or pan‑fried in a small amount of oil until browned.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen tenders in their original packaging in the freezer at –18 °C or lower. After opening, reseal the bag tightly to prevent freezer burn. Do not thaw and keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

grits-with-cheese-no-added-fat.title: Grits with Cheese, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Grits with cheese, no added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product made from whole grain grits, mild cheese and seasonings. It is prepared without any added vegetable or animal fats, preserving the natural taste of the grain and a subtle creamy note from the cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grits are one of the few grains naturally gluten‑free.
The cheese used is typically low‑fat cottage or processed cheese, keeping the calorie count low.
Grits contain antioxidants such as rutin, which supports vascular health.
Traditionally grits are cooked as a porridge, but the ready‑to‑eat version is convenient for on‑the‑go consumption.
Combining grits with cheese provides a complete amino‑acid profile.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Together, grits and cheese deliver about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fats makes this product suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Grits are a good source of iron and magnesium, essential for blood formation and nerve function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in grits promotes intestinal motility and helps you feel fuller longer.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Grits raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people managing diabetes.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The cheese component may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Grits contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Sodium in cheese
items.content: Some cheese varieties may have higher salt levels; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, soups, or used as a filling for wraps. If desired, heat in the microwave for 30‑40 seconds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if any off‑smell, mold, or taste change occurs.

content.title: About
content.content: Hummus is a spread made from blended chickpeas, tahini, olive oil, lemon juice and spices. The flavored version adds natural flavorings (such as paprika, garlic, herbs) that give it a vivid taste and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hummus originates from the Middle East, where it is traditionally served as an appetizer.
Chickpeas, the main ingredient, are rich in plant protein and fiber.
Tahini (sesame paste) gives hummus its creamy texture and healthy fats.
Flavored varieties often include spices like cumin, smoked paprika, or fresh herbs.
Hummus has become popular worldwide thanks to its versatility and ease of preparation.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, making hummus a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Tahini and olive oil supply monounsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes normal digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins and minerals
items.content: Hummus provides folate, iron, magnesium and zinc, important for metabolism and immunity.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Chickpeas have a low GI, so hummus does not cause sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Allergy to chickpeas or sesame
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chickpeas or tahini.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Flavored versions often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice can increase acidity, which may be problematic for those with gastritis or heartburn.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hummus can be spread on bread, used as a dip for vegetables, added to sandwiches, salads, or as a base for sauces. It also pairs well with pita, crackers, or veggie sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hummus in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. Once opened, it is usually good for 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Old fashioned is a classic cocktail that first appeared in the late 19th century. It is made with bourbon or rye whiskey, sugar, Angostura bitters and a splash of water, served over ice and garnished with an orange peel.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipe was published in the 1880s in "The Bartender's Manual".
The name "Old fashioned" comes from the phrase "old‑fashioned way", meaning "in the traditional manner".
The drink is considered one of the "five basic" cocktails (Old Fashioned, Martini, Manhattan, Daiquiri, Margarita).
Traditionally a sugar cube is used, muddled with bitters and a little water.
In the 2020s Old fashioned experienced a revival thanks to its popularity in TV series and bar culture.

items.title: Moderate alcohol consumption
items.content: Moderate intake of whiskey may support cardiovascular health due to its polyphenol content.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: A small serving can promote relaxation and lower stress levels.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Bourbon contains antioxidants such as ellagic acid that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Excessive alcohol intake leads to liver problems, dependence and other health issues.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Sugar adds calories and can affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol may amplify the effects of certain medications, so caution is advised.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Combine 2 tsp bourbon, 1 sugar cube, 2–3 dashes of Angostura bitters and a splash of water. Muddle the sugar, add ice (usually one large cube) and stir. Garnish with an orange peel, expressing its oils over the glass before dropping it in.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store alcoholic beverages in a cool, dark place. Keep the bourbon bottle upright, away from direct sunlight.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-poultry-resta.title: Pasta with cream sauce and poultry

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and poultry is a classic combination of tender noodles, a velvety cream sauce, and juicy poultry meat (usually chicken or turkey). The dish is popular in restaurants for its mild flavor, creamy texture, and balanced protein‑carbohydrate ratio.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter, and Parmesan, giving it a distinctive aroma.
In Italy, flat pasta shapes such as fettuccine or tagliatelle are traditionally used because they hold the sauce well.
The dish can be adapted by swapping chicken for turkey, duck, or even rabbit.
Herbs like basil, parsley, or sage are frequently added to the sauce for extra flavor.
Some regions incorporate mushrooms such as button or porcini to boost umami.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Poultry provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from cream
items.content: The cream sauce supplies calcium for bone health and vitamin D that aids its absorption.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Durum‑wheat pasta releases energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both poultry and whole‑grain pasta contain B6 and B12, important for nervous system function.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Poultry provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Cream sauce can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats; portion control is advised for weight‑watchers.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream and butter may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to milk should avoid this dish.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces or added cheese can raise salt content; monitor added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, topped with the cream sauce and sliced sautéed poultry. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, and a pinch of black pepper. The dish is eaten with a fork (and a spoon for extra sauce if desired).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. The cream sauce may separate; gently reheat and stir before serving. Freezing is possible but may alter the sauce texture, so it’s best to freeze only the pasta without the sauce.

content.title: About
content.content: The “Italian Wedding” is a traditional thick tomato soup that originated in Italy at the beginning of the 20th century. The recipe blends ripe tomatoes, fragrant basil, olive oil, garlic, and a pinch of dried herbs. It is served hot, often accompanied by crunchy croutons or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded recipe appeared in a 1903 cookbook, which gave the soup its name.
It became popular at wedding banquets in Naples, where it was served in honor of the newlyweds.
A small amount of sugar is traditionally added to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.
The original version used only olive juice pressed from olives, not oil.
The “Italian Wedding” soup is considered a predecessor of modern basil tomato soups.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil contributes monounsaturated fats that help lower “bad” cholesterol levels.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: A serving contains about 80 kcal, making it a suitable option for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from tomatoes boosts the body’s immune defenses.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or basil.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If prepared with store‑bought broth or added salt, the sodium level can become high; monitor salt usage.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes may aggravate heartburn in people with acid reflux.

items.title: Olive oil
items.content: Large amounts of oil can increase the calorie load and cause discomfort for those with gallbladder issues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, typically with croutons, a sprinkle of grated Parmesan, or fresh basil. For a richer texture, a splash of cream can be added.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a little water or broth to restore the desired consistency.
